title: Tsunami Safety
description: Tsunamis are giant ocean waves caused by underwater earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, or landslides. Recognizing warning signs and knowing how to respond can save lives in coastal areas.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: A tsunami is a series of enormous ocean waves caused by sudden displacement of large volumes of water, typically due to underwater earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, or landslides. Tsunami waves can travel across oceans at high speeds and grow to enormous heights when they reach shallow coastal waters. Unlike normal waves, tsunamis do not stop at the shore but continue inland, causing massive destruction. India's coastal regions are vulnerable to tsunamis, particularly the eastern coast.

sections.heading: Natural Warning Signs
sections.content: If you are near the coast and feel a strong earthquake that lasts for more than 20 seconds, move to higher ground immediately. Watch for the ocean receding unusually far from the shore—this is a natural warning sign that a tsunami is approaching. Listen for roaring ocean sounds similar to a train or aircraft. If you observe any of these signs, do not wait for official warnings—evacuate immediately. Tsunamis can arrive within minutes of the triggering event, leaving little time for official warnings.

sections.heading: Before a Tsunami
sections.content: Know if you live, work, or play in a tsunami hazard zone. Identify evacuation routes to higher ground or inland areas at least 2 kilometers away from the coast. Practice evacuation drills with your family. Prepare an emergency kit with food, water, medications, flashlight, battery-powered radio, first aid supplies, and important documents. Keep the kit in an easily accessible location. Know the local tsunami warning signs and official alert systems. If you are a boat owner, plan how to move your boat to deeper water if time permits.

sections.heading: During a Tsunami
sections.content: Move immediately to higher ground or inland if you feel a strong earthquake, see the ocean recede, or receive an official tsunami warning. Do not wait for all waves to pass—tsunamis consist of multiple waves that can arrive hours apart. Never go to the shore to watch a tsunami. If you cannot evacuate to high ground, go to the upper level of a sturdy concrete building. If you are in a boat in deep water, do not return to port—move to deeper water if possible. If you are on the beach and cannot reach high ground, climb a strong tree if no other shelter is available.

sections.heading: After a Tsunami
sections.content: Stay away from coastal areas until officials declare it safe. Tsunami danger can last for several hours after the first wave. Check for injuries and provide first aid to those in need. Listen to radio or TV for the latest emergency information. Avoid disaster areas as your presence might interfere with rescue operations. Do not drink tap water until officials confirm it is safe. Use boiled or bottled water. Help injured or trapped persons if you can do so without putting yourself in danger. Be prepared for aftershocks if the tsunami was caused by an earthquake.

sections.heading: Safety Precautions
sections.content: Never ignore tsunami warnings or evacuation orders. Do not assume the danger is over after the first wave—tsunamis can have multiple waves over several hours. Stay away from debris in the water as it can be dangerous. Avoid downed power lines and report them to authorities. Do not enter damaged buildings until they have been inspected. Be cautious of contaminated water and food after a tsunami. Follow all instructions from emergency responders and local authorities. If you are in a safe location, stay there until the all-clear is given.
